questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What counts as a single stroke
questions.learningObjective: Identify which mark in a written character is one stroke
questions.stem: In a stroke-count table, a calligrapher counts the left vertical of 木 as one continuous mark; how many strokes is that single vertical line?

options.text: It counts as one stroke because the brush never lifts from the paper.
It counts as two strokes since the line has a top and bottom half.
options.misconception: splits a continuous mark into two by position

options.text: It counts as zero strokes because verticals are radicals not strokes.
options.misconception: confuses radical with stroke classification

options.text: It counts as three strokes because the table lists every pen lift.
options.misconception: treats pen lifts as separate counted strokes

questions.explanation: A single stroke is one continuous brush movement without lifting. The vertical line is drawn in one motion, so it is one stroke.
questions.hint: Count brush movements, not line segments.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The hook is not a separate stroke
questions.learningObjective: Recognize that a hook belongs to its parent stroke
questions.stem: A student reads a data table and sees that 乙 is listed with one stroke; explain why the final hook does not add a second stroke.

answer.exemplar: The hook is the terminal flick of the same brush movement, so the whole mark is drawn without lifting and counts as one stroke.

questions.explanation: The hook is not a separate pen movement but the ending of the same stroke. Lifting the brush would create a new stroke, which does not happen here.
questions.hint: A hook ends one stroke, not starts another.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A turning stroke counted once
questions.learningObjective: Count a stroke that changes direction as one stroke

stimulus.body: A data table lists the character 九 as having two strokes: one horizontal and one hook-like turn. The second mark bends without lifting.

questions.stem: Using the table above, how many strokes does the turning mark in 九 count as?

options.text: It counts as two strokes because the direction changes midway through.
options.misconception: counts direction changes as new strokes

options.text: It counts as one stroke because the brush stays down through the turn.
It counts as zero strokes because turns are decorative flourishes.
options.misconception: dismisses turning marks as non-strokes

options.text: It counts as three strokes because the table adds a lift at the bend.
options.misconception: invents an extra pen lift at the turn

questions.explanation: A turning stroke keeps the brush on paper, so it is one stroke despite the change of direction. Counting turns as lifts is the common error.
questions.hint: Direction change without lifting is still one stroke.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Adding the parts of a character
questions.learningObjective: Sum the strokes of two parts to get a total
questions.stem: A data table shows 休 has a person radical of two strokes and a tree part of four strokes; what is the total stroke count?

options.text: Two strokes, by counting only the radical and ignoring the rest.
options.misconception: counts only the radical and ignores the rest

options.text: Six strokes, by adding one extra stroke for the join between parts.
options.misconception: adds a phantom joining stroke between parts

options.text: Six strokes, by adding the two part counts together directly.
Four strokes, by counting only the tree part and ignoring the radical.
options.misconception: counts only the phonetic part and ignores radical

questions.explanation: The total is the sum of the part counts: two plus four equals six. No extra joining stroke is added.
questions.hint: Add the part counts without extra strokes.
